title: Shared Mentor
statement: A mentorship program arranges members by badge number in a binary search tree: smaller numbers are in a member's left subtree and larger ones in the right, all distinct. The tree is given in level order with null for a missing child. Given two badge numbers a and b that are both in the tree, return the badge of their closest shared mentor: the deepest member that has both a and b in its subtree (a member counts as its own mentor).
constraints: Values are distinct and form a valid binary search tree
a and b are both in the tree (they may be equal)

examples.explanation: 2 is an ancestor of 4, so 2 is the shared mentor.

hints.content: In a general tree you would search both subtrees, but a BST tells you which way to go.
If both badges are smaller than the current member, the shared mentor is in the left subtree.
If both are larger, it is in the right subtree.
Otherwise they split here (or one of them is this member), so this member is the answer.
Walk down from the root using those three rules; no recursion or extra memory needed.

testCases.explanation: 2 is an ancestor of 4, so 2 is the shared mentor.
Deep nodes on the same side of the root.

solutions.title: Compare search paths
solutions.intuition: The shared mentor is the last member that the search paths to a and to b have in common.
solutions.approach: Record the path of values from the root to a and to b using BST search, then take the last common value.
solutions.pseudocode: pa = search path to a; pb = search path to b; i = longest common prefix; return pa[i-1]
commonMistakes: Returning the first difference instead of the last common value.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Storing both search paths and comparing them works and is easy to explain; it just keeps two path arrays.

solutions.title: Walk down by splitting point
solutions.intuition: The shared mentor is the first member on the way down where a and b stop being on the same side.
solutions.approach: From the root: if both values are smaller go left, if both are larger go right, otherwise return the current value.
solutions.pseudocode:
node = root
loop: if a < v and b < v: left elif a > v and b > v: right else return v
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n) to build plus O(h) to answer
commonMistakes: Using <= in the comparisons, which walks past a when a is the mentor itself.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The BST ordering means a and b stay on the same side until their shared mentor, so I walk down from the root and stop at the split point. That's O(h) per query and O(1) extra memory. In a plain binary tree I'd use a recursive search that returns which targets were found in each subtree.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: a = 2, b = 4 at 6: both smaller, go left.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: At 2: a equals the value, so they split here. Return 2.
